content: The chairs of the Sub-Regional Verification Committees (SRVC) and National Verification Committees (NVC) are responsible for several critical functions. These include defining internal procedures and responsibilities for committee members in alignment with the guidelines set by the Regional Verification Commission (RVC). They are also tasked with preparing a comprehensive SRVC/NVC plan that outlines activities, timelines, expected outcomes, and the required human and financial resources. This plan must be developed in collaboration with the National Immunization Program (NIP) and the Ministry of Health and subsequently presented to the RVC for approval. Additionally, the chairs preside over SRVC/NVC meetings, which are required to occur at least twice annually, and attend RVC or other regional meetings as necessary. The RVC, SRVC, and NVCs play an active role in advocating for measles elimination. This involves raising awareness and securing commitment from high-ranking health officials, healthcare professionals, partners, and political leaders. Advocacy efforts are conducted through various channels, including national health conferences, scientific seminars, media outlets, and personal networks. For the verification of measles elimination, countries must provide robust and well-structured evidence demonstrating that they have met the criteria for measles elimination and can sustain these achievements. This includes evidence of interrupted endemic measles virus transmission for at least 36 months under verification-standard surveillance conditions. Additional evidence may be required as needed. Pacific island countries and areas are treated as a single epidemiological block for verification purposes and must submit a joint annual progress report, similar to the process for polio eradication. Annual progress reports are mandatory for all countries, regardless of their readiness for measles elimination verification. The first reports were required in the third quarter of 2013, with subsequent reports serving as updates. When a country believes it has achieved the verification criteria, it may request official recognition. These progress reports are considered official verification documents and are assessed by the RVC. In some cases, RVC members may conduct country visits. The annual progress report must include several components: background information, a detailed description of measles epidemiology since the introduction of the measles vaccine, the quality of epidemiological and laboratory surveillance systems, population immunity data (including underserved or marginalized groups), sustainability of the national immunization program, genotyping evidence supporting the interruption of measles virus transmission, the NVC plan, and validation, comments, conclusions, and recommendations from the NVC or SRVC. Countries can utilize existing data sources to compile their annual progress reports, reducing the burden of data collection. Examples of such sources include the comprehensive multi-year plan (cMYP) for immunization, population data from the WHO/UNICEF Joint Reporting Form (JRF), epidemiological and laboratory data from national and regional measles-rubella bulletins, and information from the WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific's Measles Elimination Country Profiles. The verification process requires subnational data analysis, including second administrative level data for measles epidemiology and surveillance performance, or third administrative level data for vaccination coverage. WHO regional documents, such as the Measles-Rubella Bulletin and Country Profiles, provide useful examples for presenting subnational data. The first progress report should include a detailed history of measles control in the country, including the introduction of the first and second doses of the measles-containing vaccine (MCV1 and MCV2), changes in immunization schedules, and the evolution of strategies for measles control and elimination. This information is often available from previous national plans and should be updated as needed. Countries are expected to provide detailed descriptions of confirmed measles cases, including their location, population demographics, and any associated outbreaks. Maps and graphs can be used to present this information. For hard-to-reach populations, the report should describe efforts to reach these groups. High-quality information on recent measles outbreaks, including response actions, outcomes, and lessons learned, must also be included. The report should analyze the source and method of measles case confirmation, using epidemiological curves color-coded by endemic, unknown, imported, and import-related cases. A detailed description of clinically measles-compatible cases should also be provided, including maps, age and immunization status, clinical signs and symptoms, other possible diseases, and cases discarded by expert review committees. Information on the quality of epidemiological and laboratory surveillance systems should be presented, including actions to address any identified gaps. Population immunity should be analyzed using birth cohort data, with evidence related to underserved or marginalized groups. National data should be supplemented with third administrative level data where available. The sustainability of the national immunization program is critical for maintaining measles elimination. This includes routine immunization, supplementary immunization activities (SIAs), and surveillance with laboratory confirmation. Countries must provide national action plans and financing strategies, as well as evidence of monitoring and reviewing progress against these plans. Political commitment and sufficient resources are essential for implementing and sustaining these activities. Genotyping evidence is required to verify the absence of endemic measles virus transmission. Countries must provide information on historic and recent measles virus strains, including genotyping data and phylogenetic trees where available. Each country must develop an NVC plan that includes a roster of committee members, orientation for NVC members, annual review meetings, field visits, preparation of annual progress reports, attendance at RVC meetings, and implementation of RVC recommendations. Feedback to the NIP for action on RVC recommendations is also required. Finally, the report must include validation, comments, conclusions, and recommendations from the NVC, summarizing the outcomes of the report review process.
